messages.content: I want to develop causal speech enhancement that distinguishes whispered consonants from transient noise without fabricating speech when an acoustic event is ambiguous. What should the goal capture?

It should capture both the enhancement objective and the constraint on what the enhancement may do. The system should improve the signal while preserving whispered consonants rather than treating them as noise. At the same time, it should not turn a transient that might be noise into speech that was not present. “Causal” means the enhancement operates without relying on future audio.
So an ambiguous transient is the difficult case: it could be a whispered consonant, but enhancing it too confidently could create speech?

Yes. The distinction matters in both directions. Suppressing an actual whispered consonant risks deleting speech; interpreting noise as a consonant risks inserting speech. The goal is not simply to make the audio sound cleaner, but to improve it without introducing either kind of phonetic error beyond the stated limits.
There is also a numerical enhancement requirement. Please state it precisely.

The enhanced audio must improve SI-SDR by at least 3 dB over the noisy inputs on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises. The comparison is to the noisy inputs, and the specified evaluation conditions include both held-out whispered speech and noises that were unseen.
Does the 3 dB requirement replace the need to check consonants?

No. SI-SDR improvement is one requirement, and consonant preservation is another. Even an enhancement that reaches the ≥3 dB SI-SDR improvement would not satisfy the stated goal if its consonant deletion or insertion rate exceeds the corresponding rate for the unprocessed inputs under matched phonetic evaluation.
Can you spell out what those two consonant rates mean here without adding a new test?

A consonant deletion concerns a consonant that was present but is lost in the processed speech. A consonant insertion concerns a consonant that was not present but appears in the processed speech. The requirement is that neither rate exceed its unprocessed-input rate under matched phonetic evaluation. It does not say either rate must be zero.
If enhancement removes a noise transient but also erases a whispered consonant, how would that relate to the goal?

That illustrates why noise reduction alone is insufficient. Erasing a real whispered consonant is the kind of deletion the phonetic requirement is meant to guard against. Whether an evaluated system meets the requirement depends on the resulting deletion rate compared with the unprocessed-input rate under matched phonetic evaluation.
And if it makes an ambiguous noise burst sound like a consonant?

That illustrates the fabrication risk. If processing creates a consonant where none was present, it is the kind of insertion the goal seeks to avoid. Ambiguity is not permission to invent speech; the insertion-rate requirement checks that such errors do not increase relative to the unprocessed inputs under matched phonetic evaluation.
Is the wording asking for perfect separation of every whispered consonant and every transient noise?

No perfect event-by-event separation is stated. The goal is to distinguish whispered consonants from transient noise without fabricating speech during ambiguous events, alongside the specified evaluation requirements: ≥3 dB SI-SDR improvement over noisy inputs on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises, and consonant deletion and insertion rates that do not exceed the unprocessed-input rates under matched phonetic evaluation.
How should I read “do not exceed” if a consonant error rate happens to be equal to the unprocessed-input rate?

Equality is allowed by that wording. For each of the two rates, the processed result must be no higher than the unprocessed-input rate under matched phonetic evaluation. The requirement does not demand a reduction in either rate, though it does prohibit an increase.
Is the SI-SDR condition simply that the output has a positive SI-SDR?

No. It specifies an improvement relative to the noisy inputs: the SI-SDR improvement must be at least 3 dB on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises. A positive value by itself would not express that comparison.
What does “held-out” contribute to the statement?

It makes clear that the SI-SDR target concerns whispered speech reserved for evaluation, rather than merely speech used while developing the enhancement. “Unseen noises” likewise specifies that the target applies with noises not previously seen. The node does not specify a dataset, a particular noise type, or a procedure for computing an aggregate result.
Does calling the enhancement causal settle how it should be implemented?

No. Causality constrains the information available to the enhancement: it cannot rely on future audio to process the current audio. The goal does not prescribe an architecture, a decision rule for ambiguous events, or a particular implementation.
Then the intended balance is to improve distortion while not trading away consonant accuracy or adding imagined speech?

Exactly. The SI-SDR target addresses improvement over the noisy inputs; the matched phonetic comparison limits consonant deletion and insertion. Both matter for whispered speech, where a transient may be difficult to interpret and aggressive processing could either remove a consonant or make noise sound like one.
Give me one compact statement that keeps all the conditions intact.

Develop causal speech enhancement that distinguishes whispered consonants from transient noise without fabricating speech during ambiguous acoustic events; improve SI-SDR by ≥3 dB over noisy inputs on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises, while ensuring consonant deletion and insertion rates do not exceed the unprocessed-input rates under matched phonetic evaluation.
What approach would fit the causal enhancement goal we discussed?

A proposed approach is a zero-lookahead causal mask estimator with consonant/transient discriminators and uncertainty-gated attenuation. When an acoustic event remains ambiguous, the approach is to preserve the input rather than synthesize speech to resolve the ambiguity.
How does zero-lookahead make the proposal causal?

Zero-lookahead means the estimator does not use future audio to decide how to process the audio currently available. That is consistent with causal enhancement. The proposal does not specify the estimator’s architecture or other timing details.
What role does the mask estimator play?

It estimates how to attenuate parts of the input as enhancement proceeds. Framing the proposal as masking keeps the input signal central: the method is intended to adjust what is there, rather than generate a speech signal to fill in uncertain events. The proposal does not specify a particular mask representation.
Why add consonant/transient discriminators?

They address the key ambiguity: a short acoustic event could be a whispered consonant or transient noise. Their proposed role is to inform that distinction so attenuation need not treat every transient as noise. Calling for discriminators states the function they should serve; it does not, by itself, prescribe how they are built or establish that they will always classify an event correctly.
And what is uncertainty-gated attenuation meant to do?

It makes uncertainty relevant to whether attenuation is applied. When the evidence does not clearly distinguish a whispered consonant from a noise transient, the proposed behavior is to preserve the ambiguous input instead of aggressively attenuating it or synthesizing speech. No numerical uncertainty threshold or exact gating rule is specified.
Does preserving an ambiguous event mean treating it as definitely speech?

No. Preserving the input acknowledges that the event is unresolved; it does not label the event as speech. The proposal avoids making the stronger, unsupported move of constructing a consonant from an event that might be noise.
Could leaving the ambiguous input in place also leave some noise in the output?

It could. The proposal favors retaining an uncertain event over removing a possible whispered consonant or fabricating speech to explain it. That tradeoff is part of the proposed handling of ambiguity, not a claim that every ambiguous event will be cleanly separated.
Is uncertainty-gated attenuation the same as always leaving transients untouched?

No. The proposal is to use consonant/transient discrimination and gate attenuation according to uncertainty. It specifically calls for preserving ambiguous input; it does not say that all transients are ambiguous or that attenuation is never applied to them.
How is this different from deciding that any consonant-like burst should be enhanced into a clearer consonant?

That decision would risk turning a noise transient into speech. Here, the proposed response to unresolved evidence is not to synthesize a clearer consonant. The mask estimator and uncertainty-gated attenuation are meant to work with the available input while respecting that uncertainty.
Does the proposal guarantee the ≥3 dB SI-SDR improvement we specified?

No. The ≥3 dB SI-SDR improvement over noisy inputs on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises remains a goal to evaluate. The proposal describes a way to pursue causal enhancement; it is not a reported result or a guarantee that the target has been reached.
Nor does it automatically guarantee the consonant error limits, right?

Right. Preserving ambiguous input is intended to address deletion and fabrication risks, but its effect must not be assumed. Under matched phonetic evaluation, consonant deletion and insertion rates would still need to be no higher than their respective unprocessed-input rates.
Could the two evaluation requirements pull in different directions?

They can express different demands on the same processing decision. Strong attenuation might improve a signal-distortion measure while risking deletion of a whispered consonant; treating an uncertain event as speech might risk an insertion. The proposal’s uncertainty gate is a way to approach those decisions, not proof that both requirements will be satisfied.
When you say “preserve the input,” do you mean the entire recording must remain unprocessed whenever one event is uncertain?

No. The phrase concerns the ambiguous input event: the proposal is to preserve it rather than synthesize speech in its place. It does not require leaving an entire recording unchanged, and it does not specify the exact extent of preservation around an event.
Is there a particular discriminator design or training procedure implied?

No particular design or training procedure is stated. The proposal names consonant/transient discriminators for their intended role, together with a zero-lookahead causal mask estimator and uncertainty-gated attenuation. Further implementation choices would go beyond what is specified here.
So the central rule for an unclear consonant-versus-noise event is restraint?

Yes. In this proposal, uncertainty should restrain attenuation, and it should not be resolved by synthesizing speech. The input remains the reference for an ambiguous event while the estimator operates causally, without future audio.
Can you put the proposal in one sentence without implying it has already been validated?

Propose a zero-lookahead causal mask estimator with consonant/transient discriminators and uncertainty-gated attenuation, preserving ambiguous input rather than synthesizing speech; whether it meets the SI-SDR and consonant-error requirements remains to be evaluated.
Which confidence threshold preserves whispered /t/ bursts while suppressing keyboard clicks at 0 dB SNR?

There isn’t enough information to name a numerical threshold. The question identifies the desired balance at 0 dB SNR, but gives no confidence values or outcomes showing where whispered /t/ bursts and keyboard clicks fall relative to a threshold.
What would a threshold need to accomplish in that case?

It would need to allow whispered /t/ bursts to remain audible while permitting suppression of keyboard clicks, specifically at 0 dB SNR. A threshold that suppresses the clicks but also removes /t/ bursts would not achieve both parts of the question.
Could I simply ask for a higher confidence threshold?

Not without specifying what the confidence score means and what happens when it crosses the threshold. If it measures confidence that an event is noise, raising the threshold could make suppression more selective. If it measures confidence that an event is a consonant, the interpretation could differ. The question alone does not define that direction.
The setting is still 0 dB SNR. Does that determine the number?

No. The 0 dB SNR condition is important to the question, but it does not specify a confidence scale or show how either whispered /t/ bursts or keyboard clicks are scored. It cannot by itself determine the threshold.
Why single out whispered /t/ bursts rather than just saying consonants?

It makes the preservation question specific: the threshold must be considered in relation to whispered /t/ bursts, not consonants in general. Likewise, the suppression target here is keyboard clicks, not every transient noise. A threshold shown to work for some other event would not, on that basis alone, answer this question.
Would a threshold that keeps both the /t/ bursts and the keyboard clicks answer it?
No. That would satisfy preservation of the whispered /t/ bursts but not suppression of the keyboard clicks. The question asks for a threshold that does both at 0 dB SNR.
What if the threshold removes both?
That would suppress the keyboard clicks but fail to preserve the whispered /t/ bursts. Neither one-sided result identifies the requested threshold.
Could one threshold be inferred from the fact that both are short events?

No. Their being brief does not provide the missing confidence values or show that a threshold separates them. The difficulty posed by the question is precisely whether the confidence measure distinguishes the whispered /t/ bursts from keyboard clicks at 0 dB SNR.
How would uncertainty-gated attenuation relate to this question?

The confidence threshold would govern how the gate responds to uncertainty, once the score and gating direction are defined. For this question, the relevant behavior is preservation of whispered /t/ bursts alongside suppression of keyboard clicks at 0 dB SNR. The threshold value cannot be read off from that intended behavior alone.
Should an ambiguous event be made to sound more like a /t/ burst so it clears the threshold?

No. Making an event sound like speech would not establish that it was a whispered /t/ burst. The threshold question concerns whether the available confidence can guide attenuation while preserving actual /t/ bursts and suppressing keyboard clicks, not creating a consonant to resolve uncertainty.
Suppose the confidence scores for the two event types overlap. Would the wording still imply there is a perfect threshold?

No. The wording asks which threshold achieves the desired distinction; it does not establish that a single threshold can perfectly separate the two. Without the scores and corresponding preservation and suppression outcomes, even the existence of such a threshold is undetermined.
What information is missing before someone could give a defensible number?

At minimum, they would need the definition and scale of the confidence score, which side of the threshold triggers attenuation, and evidence of how candidate thresholds affect whispered /t/ bursts and keyboard clicks at 0 dB SNR. None of those values or outcomes is supplied here.
Can you answer the original question as directly as possible, then?

The confidence threshold is not specified and cannot be determined from the information given. It would have to preserve whispered /t/ bursts while suppressing keyboard clicks at 0 dB SNR; no numerical value or demonstrated threshold is available here.
For the threshold question, I have a hypothesis: a 0.65 consonant-posterior threshold should retain ≥90% of whispered /t/ bursts while enabling ≥70% keyboard-click attenuation at 0 dB SNR.

That states a specific candidate threshold and two outcomes to test. At 0 dB SNR, the hypothesis is that a consonant-posterior threshold of 0.65 will retain at least 90% of whispered /t/ bursts while enabling at least 70% keyboard-click attenuation. “Should” is important: these are predicted outcomes, not reported measurements.
Why specify that it is a consonant-posterior threshold?

It identifies what the 0.65 value applies to: a score concerning whether an event is a consonant. Without that label, 0.65 could be mistaken for a threshold on a different confidence measure. The hypothesis does not specify how the posterior is produced or the exact rule that uses it.
Does 0.65 mean we already know that whispered /t/ bursts score above it?

No. The hypothesis predicts retention of ≥90% of whispered /t/ bursts with that threshold, but it supplies no observed posterior scores or retention results. The value is a candidate, not evidence that the predicted retention has occurred.
How should I read the 90% figure?

It is a minimum retention target for whispered /t/ bursts: at least 90% should be retained under the stated 0 dB SNR condition. It is not a claim of perfect retention, and it is not yet an observed rate.
And the 70% figure is about a different event?

Yes. The ≥70% figure concerns attenuation of keyboard clicks. It is paired with, but distinct from, the ≥90% retention target for whispered /t/ bursts. The hypothesis asks whether the 0.65 threshold can support both outcomes at 0 dB SNR.
Could we say that 70% of keyboard clicks are eliminated?

That would add a meaning the hypothesis does not specify. It says “≥70% keyboard-click attenuation,” not that ≥70% of clicks disappear altogether. The exact way attenuation is quantified would need to be defined before treating those as equivalent.
Does 0 dB SNR apply to both parts of the prediction?
Yes. The hypothesis places both the whispered /t/ retention target and the keyboard-click attenuation target at 0 dB SNR. It makes no prediction here about other SNR conditions.
If retention reaches 90% but keyboard-click attenuation falls short of 70%, would the whole hypothesis hold?

No. Both predicted minimums are part of the hypothesis at the 0.65 consonant-posterior threshold and 0 dB SNR. Meeting the whispered /t/ retention target alone would not establish the keyboard-click attenuation target.
What if the keyboard-click attenuation target is met but too many whispered /t/ bursts are lost?

That would likewise fall short of the combined prediction. The threshold is proposed as a way to balance preservation and attenuation; the hypothesis requires ≥90% retention of whispered /t/ bursts as well as ≥70% keyboard-click attenuation.
Is 0.65 being presented as the proven best threshold?
No. It is a hypothesized threshold for these two stated outcomes at 0 dB SNR. Nothing here establishes that it works, that it is optimal, or how it compares with other threshold values.
Would meeting those two percentages prove that ambiguous events never become fabricated speech?

No. Those percentages address retention of whispered /t/ bursts and attenuation of keyboard clicks. They do not, by themselves, establish what happens to every ambiguous event or whether speech is ever fabricated. The hypothesis should be kept to the outcomes it actually predicts.
Can you phrase it without turning the prediction into a result?

A 0.65 consonant-posterior threshold is hypothesized to retain ≥90% of whispered /t/ bursts while enabling ≥70% keyboard-click attenuation at 0 dB SNR. Those figures are targets to test, not measured performance.
How should we examine the threshold question rather than relying on the 0.65 hypothesis alone?

The plan is to sweep consonant-posterior thresholds from 0.45 to 0.85 on held-out 0 dB whisper/keyboard mixtures. Across the sweep, compare whispered /t/ retention, keyboard-click suppression, SI-SDR, and consonant errors. That would show how the relevant outcomes vary with the threshold rather than treating one proposed value as an observed answer.
Is 0.65 included in that range?
Yes. The proposed 0.65 threshold lies between 0.45 and 0.85, so the sweep can examine it alongside other thresholds in the range. The plan does not report how it performs.
Why compare /t/ retention and click suppression together?

They represent the two sides of the threshold question. Retaining whispered /t/ bursts matters because they are speech; suppressing keyboard clicks matters because they are the transient noise of interest. Looking at only one outcome could hide a loss in the other.
Where does SI-SDR fit if those two outcomes are the immediate concern?

SI-SDR adds a signal-level enhancement comparison. The sweep is not just asking whether /t/ bursts remain or clicks are suppressed; it also compares SI-SDR across thresholds. The plan lists the measure but does not supply SI-SDR results.
And why include consonant errors separately from /t/ retention?

The /t/ retention comparison focuses on the particular whispered burst named in the threshold question. Consonant errors provide a broader phonetic check, including the concern that processing could delete consonants or introduce ones that were not present. The plan calls for comparing those errors without specifying results.
Does the plan say to test at several SNRs?
No. This sweep is specified for held-out whisper/keyboard mixtures at 0 dB SNR. It does not state that other SNRs are included.
Does “held-out” mean these are the same mixtures used to choose the estimator?

No such identity is stated. “Held-out” indicates mixtures reserved for this evaluation rather than mixtures used in development. The plan gives no further details about how they were assembled or divided.
Are the thresholds spaced at fixed intervals?
The plan gives the range, 0.45–0.85, but not a step size or a list of individual thresholds. A specific spacing would be an additional detail, not something established by the plan.
What should comparing all four measures help us see?

It should help reveal how the candidate thresholds balance preservation of whispered /t/ bursts, suppression of keyboard clicks, SI-SDR, and consonant errors on the specified held-out 0 dB mixtures. The comparison is planned; no balance or preferred threshold has been demonstrated yet.
If one threshold suppresses clicks strongly, is that enough to answer the original question?

No. The question also asks that whispered /t/ bursts be preserved. The sweep includes /t/ retention precisely so click suppression is not considered in isolation, and it also compares SI-SDR and consonant errors.
Could the sweep establish that the 0.65 prediction is correct just because 0.65 is in the range?
No. Inclusion means the candidate can be examined. Establishing its predicted behavior would require the measured outcomes; the sweep is a plan, not a report of those outcomes.
Do these whisper/keyboard mixtures cover every unseen noise in the broader enhancement goal?

The plan specifies held-out 0 dB whisper/keyboard mixtures. It does not say this sweep covers every unseen noise or every condition in the broader goal. Its comparisons are tied to the mixtures and SNR stated here.
Would consonant errors in the sweep be interchangeable with SI-SDR?
No. SI-SDR and consonant errors address different aspects of the output. Comparing both helps avoid treating a signal-level improvement as a complete account of what happened to the consonants.
Can you restate the plan without suggesting any threshold has already won?

Sweep thresholds from 0.45 to 0.85 on held-out whisper/keyboard mixtures at 0 dB SNR, comparing whispered /t/ retention, keyboard-click suppression, SI-SDR, and consonant errors. The plan specifies what to compare, not which threshold will perform best or whether any candidate meets the desired outcomes.
For the threshold evaluation, what activity are we specifying now?

Sweep thresholds from 0.45 to 0.85 across 400 held-out whisper/keyboard mixtures at 0 dB SNR. Measure whispered /t/ retention, keyboard-click attenuation, SI-SDR, and consonant errors across the sweep.
Is 400 the number of thresholds?
No. It is the number of held-out 0 dB whisper/keyboard mixtures. The activity specifies the threshold range, 0.45–0.85, but not how many individual threshold values to use within it.
Should I describe the mixtures as just whispered speech?
That would leave out part of the condition. They are whisper/keyboard mixtures: the activity concerns whispered speech mixed with keyboard noise, at 0 dB SNR.
What are we measuring to tell whether whispered /t/ bursts survive?
The specified measure is /t/ retention. It directly addresses preservation of the whispered /t/ bursts as the threshold varies. The activity does not yet provide retention values.
And for the keyboard sounds?

Measure keyboard-click attenuation. That tracks what happens to the clicks across the threshold sweep. It should not be reported as a measured percentage or as complete removal unless the measurements actually support that description.
Why are SI-SDR and consonant errors both on the list?

They capture different aspects of the processed audio. SI-SDR measures signal-level enhancement, while consonant errors check the phonetic consequences. Neither one alone substitutes for the specific /t/ retention and click-attenuation measurements in this activity.
Does measuring consonant errors mean we can assume they stay no higher than in the unprocessed inputs?

No. Measuring them is how that question can be examined; it does not establish the outcome. The activity states what to measure, not the resulting error rates or their comparison with the unprocessed inputs.
Does this activity include the proposed 0.65 threshold?

Yes. A threshold of 0.65 lies within the 0.45–0.85 sweep range. The measurements can therefore address the prediction about that candidate, but its /t/ retention and click attenuation cannot be stated as results yet.
Would the measurements at 0.65 speak to the predicted ≥90% retention and ≥70% click attenuation?

Yes. The measured /t/ retention and keyboard-click attenuation at 0.65, under the specified 0 dB condition, are the relevant outcomes for examining those two predicted minimums. The activity does not say whether either minimum is achieved.
If the sweep has those measurements, can we already call 0.65 the selected threshold?
No. Specifying the sweep and its measurements does not select a threshold or report any comparison results. The activity leaves the outcome open.
Is this an evaluation across all noise types?
No. The activity specifies 400 held-out 0 dB whisper/keyboard mixtures. It does not say that other noise types or SNR conditions are included.
Do we know the step size between 0.45 and 0.85?
No step size is specified. Only the range to sweep is given, so naming particular intermediate values beyond the already discussed 0.65 candidate would add detail not supplied here.
How can I state the activity without making it sound like completed results?

State it as an evaluation activity: sweep thresholds 0.45–0.85 across 400 held-out 0 dB whisper/keyboard mixtures, measuring /t/ retention, keyboard-click attenuation, SI-SDR, and consonant errors. That identifies the conditions and measurements without claiming any observed performance.
What did the evaluation show at the 0.65 consonant-posterior threshold?

Across 400 held-out whisper/keyboard mixtures at 0 dB SNR, whispered /t/ retention was 82% at the 0.65 threshold, despite 74% keyboard-click attenuation. The retention result missed the predicted 90%.
How far below the predicted retention was that?
The observed 82% retention was 8 percentage points below the predicted 90%. That is a percentage-point difference, not a claim about how many individual /t/ bursts were lost.
Does the 74% figure mean 74% of keyboard clicks disappeared entirely?
No. The reported result is 74% click attenuation. It does not say that 74% of individual clicks disappeared, or define attenuation as complete removal.
Could I describe this as a clean success because the clicks were attenuated?

That would overlook the other observed outcome. The result pairs 74% click attenuation with 82% whispered /t/ retention, which missed the predicted 90%. Click attenuation alone does not erase that retention shortfall.
Does 82% retention tell us the consonant deletion rate under matched phonetic evaluation?

Not by itself. This result reports /t/ retention at 0.65, but it does not give a matched phonetic consonant-deletion rate or its comparison with the unprocessed inputs. Those should not be inferred from the retention percentage alone.
What about consonant insertions?
No consonant-insertion result is reported here. The 82% /t/ retention and 74% click attenuation do not establish an insertion rate.
Do we have the SI-SDR result for these 400 mixtures?
Not in this result. It reports /t/ retention and click attenuation at 0.65, but no SI-SDR value or improvement over the noisy inputs.
Since this was a sweep, can we say a different threshold performed better?

No comparison with another threshold is given here. The reported evidence concerns the 0.65 threshold; it does not identify a better threshold or show how retention and attenuation changed elsewhere in the 0.45–0.85 range.
Does the result tell us why the /t/ retention was lower than predicted?

No cause is established. The result says retention was 82% rather than the predicted 90%, alongside 74% click attenuation. It does not identify which acoustic events or processing decisions account for the shortfall.
Is the 82% figure a result across the 400 mixtures, or does it mean exactly 82% in every mixture?
It is reported across the 400 mixtures. Nothing here says retention was 82% in each individual mixture or describes how results varied among them.
Can we generalize these numbers to other noises or SNRs?
Not from this result alone. The stated evaluation condition is 400 held-out whisper/keyboard mixtures at 0 dB SNR. No outcome for other noises or SNRs is reported here.
Then what is the precise takeaway, without inferring a new threshold or a cause?

At the 0.65 consonant-posterior threshold, /t/ retention was 82% across 400 held-out 0 dB whisper/keyboard mixtures, despite 74% keyboard-click attenuation. That misses the predicted 90% /t/ retention; the result does not specify why or identify a preferable threshold.
I want to consider a lower consonant-posterior threshold for the whispered /t/ and keyboard-click question. What is the new hypothesis?

The hypothesis is that lowering the posterior threshold to 0.55 should retain ≥90% of whispered /t/ bursts while attenuating ≥60% of keyboard clicks. These are predicted outcomes, not measured results.
Is 0.55 the threshold, rather than a measured retention rate?
Yes. The proposed consonant-posterior threshold is 0.55. The predicted outcomes at that threshold are at least 90% whispered /t/ retention and at least 60% keyboard-click attenuation.
How does this relate to the threshold question at 0 dB SNR?

It offers a candidate answer to the question of preserving whispered /t/ bursts while suppressing keyboard clicks at 0 dB SNR. The hypothesis does not establish that 0.55 achieves those outcomes; it states what the lower threshold is expected to do.
Can I say lowering the threshold will definitely recover the /t/ bursts?
No. “Should retain ≥90%” is a prediction. It does not guarantee that lowering the threshold to 0.55 will produce that retention in an evaluation.
What exactly does the ≥90% apply to?
It applies to retention of whispered /t/ bursts. It is not a claim that every consonant is retained, nor that every individual /t/ burst survives.
And is ≥60% a target for how many clicks vanish?
The wording is ≥60% keyboard-click attenuation, not that at least 60% of individual clicks vanish entirely. The hypothesis does not specify that those are equivalent.
Does the lower threshold mean we are giving up on suppressing keyboard clicks?

No. The hypothesis still predicts attenuation of at least 60% of keyboard clicks. It asks whether a 0.55 threshold can preserve whispered /t/ bursts while continuing to attenuate clicks, rather than pursuing preservation alone.
Does it say 0.55 is the best possible threshold?
No. It names 0.55 as a candidate and predicts two minimum outcomes. It does not establish optimality or report how 0.55 compares with other thresholds.
Would meeting the click-attenuation target alone confirm the hypothesis?
No. Both predictions matter: ≥90% retention of whispered /t/ bursts and ≥60% keyboard-click attenuation. A result meeting only one of them would not meet the combined prediction.
Does this hypothesis tell us whether SI-SDR improves by ≥3 dB?
No. It makes predictions about whispered /t/ retention and keyboard-click attenuation. It supplies no SI-SDR result and does not establish the broader ≥3 dB improvement requirement.
Nor does it establish consonant deletion and insertion rates relative to the unprocessed input?

Correct. The predicted /t/ retention is specific to whispered /t/ bursts, and click attenuation concerns the noise event. Neither prediction, by itself, establishes that consonant deletion and insertion rates do not exceed the unprocessed-input rates under matched phonetic evaluation.
Could we state the idea without explaining why lowering the threshold would work?

Yes. The hypothesis states an expected outcome, not a demonstrated mechanism: a 0.55 consonant-posterior threshold should retain ≥90% of whispered /t/ bursts while attenuating ≥60% of keyboard clicks. Whether it does so remains an open question.
How do we evaluate the 0.55 consonant-posterior threshold?

Evaluate 0.55 on 200 fresh whisper/keyboard mixtures at 0 dB SNR. Measure whispered /t/ retention, keyboard-click attenuation, consonant errors, and SI-SDR. This specifies the evaluation activity, not its results.
Does 200 refer to the number of threshold settings?
No. It refers to 200 fresh mixtures. The activity evaluates one specified threshold, 0.55, rather than describing another threshold sweep.
What does “fresh” tell us about those mixtures?
It identifies them as fresh mixtures for this evaluation. The activity does not give further details about how they were made or selected, so those details should not be assumed.
Is the 0 dB condition just for the keyboard clicks?
No. The evaluation condition is 0 dB SNR for the whisper/keyboard mixtures as a whole. The activity does not specify separate SNR conditions for individual events.
Why measure /t/ retention specifically?

It directly addresses whether whispered /t/ bursts are preserved at the 0.55 threshold. The associated hypothesis predicts ≥90% retention, but this activity does not yet say what the measured retention will be.
And keyboard-click attenuation tests the other part of that hypothesis?

Yes. The hypothesis predicts ≥60% keyboard-click attenuation alongside ≥90% whispered /t/ retention. Measuring both on the 200 fresh 0 dB mixtures lets those two predictions be examined without assuming either is met.
Does “click attenuation” mean counting how many clicks disappear completely?

Not necessarily. The activity calls for measuring keyboard-click attenuation; it does not define that measure as the fraction of clicks removed entirely. It would be inaccurate to equate those descriptions without a stated definition.
What additional question do the consonant-error measurements address?

They address phonetic effects beyond the specified /t/ retention measure, including the concern that enhancement might lose or introduce consonants. The activity calls for measuring consonant errors but gives no error rates or conclusions about them.
Could /t/ retention alone stand in for all consonant errors?
No. /t/ retention concerns the whispered /t/ bursts specifically. It does not, by itself, describe all consonant errors, which is why consonant errors are listed separately.
Why include SI-SDR as well?

SI-SDR captures a signal-level aspect of enhancement that /t/ retention, click attenuation, and consonant errors do not replace. Measuring it alongside the other outcomes avoids reducing the evaluation to only one kind of effect. No SI-SDR value is supplied in this activity.
Can we already say the 0.55 threshold meets the predicted percentages because this evaluation is being conducted?

No. Evaluating a threshold does not establish its performance. The /t/ retention and click-attenuation measurements would be needed to determine whether the predicted ≥90% and ≥60% levels are reached.
Does the activity establish that consonant deletion and insertion rates stay below the unprocessed-input rates?
No. It specifies measurement of consonant errors, not their results or a comparison with the unprocessed inputs. Such a conclusion cannot be drawn from the activity alone.
What about performance with other noises or at other SNRs?
This activity is limited to 200 fresh whisper/keyboard mixtures at 0 dB SNR. It does not report or specify an evaluation with other noises or at other SNRs.
Please give me the precise activity statement without implying that any measurements are already known.

Evaluate the 0.55 consonant-posterior threshold on 200 fresh 0 dB whisper/keyboard mixtures, measuring whispered /t/ retention, keyboard-click attenuation, consonant errors, and SI-SDR. The activity specifies what to measure, not the outcomes.
What did the evaluation of the 0.55 consonant-posterior threshold show?

Across 200 fresh whisper/keyboard mixtures at 0 dB SNR, the 0.55 threshold retained 92% of whispered /t/ bursts and attenuated 63% of keyboard clicks. Those observations support the revised threshold hypothesis for these two outcomes.
How do those results relate to the predicted levels?

The hypothesis predicted at least 90% whispered /t/ retention and at least 60% keyboard-click attenuation. The observed 92% retention and 63% attenuation meet both predicted minimums on the 200 fresh mixtures.
